newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico, U.S. sign declarations on drugs, migration.
newsitem.headline: Mexico, U.S. sign declarations on drugs, migration.

text.p: The United States and Mexico agreed on Tuesday to step up their war on drug traffickers and increase cooperation along their 2,000-mile (3,200 km) long joint border.

A Declaration of Alliance Against Drugs signed by Presidents Bill Clinton and Ernesto Zedillo during Clinton's visit to Mexico committed the U.S. and Mexican cabinets to agreeing a common anti-drug strategy by the end of the year.
The United States will also try to cut demand for illegal drugs at home.

"We want every U.S. citizen to understand that when they purchase an illegal drug, they are initiating a chain reaction whose effects are felt in Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Thailand and all the other countries that are afflicted by international drug criminals," U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey said at the conclusion of a joint U.S.-Mexican cabinet meeting here.
Clinton also emphasised the importance of reducing U.S. demand for drugs.

"For our part we in the United States know that we have to reduce our demand," Clinton said, adding that drug use had recently fallen among U.S. citizens aged 18-34 although it was rising among under-18s.
"We are devoting an enormous amount of time and effort to that problem," he added.
The document also laid out 16 specific objectives including the cutting of drug production and trafficking, the prosecution of kingpins and the seizure of drug assets to hit traffickers.
"President Clinton will review progress toward achieving these goals later this year," a White House press statement said.
U.S. authorities estimate that over 70 percent of the illegal drugs entering their country come through Mexico, where powerful cartels flourish and drug corruption of police is rampant.

Marking a concession by Zedillo, the statement said the Mexican government "is now willing, in 'exceptional' cases of a particularly heinous nature, to consider and undertake extradition of Mexican citizens".

Mexico has traditionally refused to extradite its own citizens to the United States, although last year Zedillo's government slipped three Mexican suspects across the border with minimal publicity to face an American trial.
The two governments also agreed to amend their extradition treaty to allow individuals to be tried in both countries prior to the completion of their sentence in either country.
Helping Mexico's efforts against powerful drug cartels, the Clinton administration agreed to help trace illegal guns and to regulate more closely the export of weapons, ammunition and explosives.
The United States and Mexico will also press for a hemispheric agreement outlawing illegal arms trading.

The two countries signed an agreement to exchange more information about currency transactions to combat money laundering. U.S. computers and training will also be provided to Mexico's Finance Ministry to help it track down launderers.
On the delicate issue of their long joint border, the presidents agreed a joint statement calling for protection for migrants' rights as well as redoubled efforts to stop criminal aliens.

"Our shared vision of the border is founded on principles of cooperation, orderly and legal movement of goods and people, joint economic activities and mutual respect for sovereignty, public safety and human rights", the White House statement said.
